skunk-removal.intro: Duncan's skunks work its subdivisions. This Spartanburg County growth town along the I-85 corridor is street after street of newer homes with raised decks, front porches on pier footings, and lawns laid over the county's red clay and old pasture — and striped skunks have colonised the under-deck voids and crawlspace edges of those streets as thoroughly as if the builders had spec'd them as dens. The South Tyger River bottoms west of town and the drainage corridors between the phases keep the population supplied. The calls follow the suburban calendar: spray events at the back door in late winter, kits under the deck in spring, grub-digging across the irrigated lawns by fall.
skunk-removal.extendedBody:
The under-deck den and the subdivision route

A Duncan skunk job is a perimeter job. The animals den under decks and porches because the voids are dry, dark, and one step from the lawn's grubs; removing the skunk without closing the void schedules the next tenant, because skunks prospect proven dens and a deck that raised one litter advertises itself to the next female each spring. We trap the residents, then screen the full deck or porch perimeter with mesh buried at the base — skunks dig at edges, and surface screening alone is an invitation to dig two feet left. Corner lots and creek-corridor lots take the traffic first, and on those we say so plainly: your address is on the route, so your screening has to be the complete version. We will also name the grub question honestly — a lawn carrying a heavy grub load is a skunk feeding station, and treating the lawn alongside the trapping and screening is what ends the digging rather than relocating it to the flower beds.

faqs.q: A skunk sprayed our dog at the back door in Duncan. Is it living here?
faqs.a: Almost certainly under the deck, the porch, or in the crawlspace edge — repeated spray events happen at a den door, where the skunk is cornered on its own threshold at dusk. We trap the resident and screen the void with buried mesh in the same job, which ends both the spraying and the tenancy. While the trapping runs, bring the dog in before full dark and check the yard with a light first; the encounters stop being surprising the moment the routine changes, and they stop entirely when the den closes.

faqs.q: How much does skunk removal cost in Duncan?
faqs.a: It depends on the structure — one skunk under a small deck is a compact job; a long deck perimeter or a crawlspace edge on a corner lot is more screening and more time. We inspect, quote the whole job firmly before trapping starts, and the quote includes the buried-mesh screening, because trapping alone on a Duncan subdivision lot is a subscription. Removal runs under a depredation permit for your property, arranged as part of the work.

mole-removal.intro: Duncan's moles inherit its subdivisions' past. The I-85 corridor town was pasture and field within living memory, and the lawns of its growth subdivisions were laid over that ground — topsoil full of earthworms and grubs, in soil the builders graded loose. Eastern moles tunnel those lawns in systems that surface along the old field lines and the irrigation runs: ridged trails across the sod, rooted flower beds, soft spots that grow a little every week of the warm season. Duncan's mole calls are lawn calls — the animal is almost never a structural problem — but they are also rarely a one-mole problem, because a subdivision's connected lawns are one continuous hunting ground divided by fences a mole does not recognise.
mole-removal.extendedBody:
Subdivision systems and the campaign method

Mole work in Duncan is done by the system, not the sighting. We read the whole property for the working runs — the surface tunnels that re-inflate overnight are the feeding lines; the straighter, deeper runs along the foundation, the driveway edges, and the fence lines are the highways — and set the trap line on what is active, then return on a cycle to check, reset, and move sets as the sign shifts. The expectation is set in the first conversation: this is a campaign over weeks, priced as one programme, and the measure of progress is the ground going quiet run by run. The street matters too, and we say so: on a connected subdivision lawn-scape, a trapped-out yard next to an untouched one is a vacancy sign, so grub treatment and watering advice — the food and moisture side of the equation — come with the trapping as part of the same plan. What we do not sell is the one-visit miracle or the vibrating stake; in red clay cut with graded topsoil, the trap line on the active system is the method, and the re-checks are the evidence.

faqs.q: How much does mole removal cost in Duncan?
faqs.a: It depends on the lot and the length of the active system — a standard subdivision yard is one programme; a corner lot with runs along two fence lines and the foundation is a longer campaign. We survey first, mark the active tunneling, and quote the whole programme — setting, checking, and resetting over the weeks required — as a firm single price. If your lawn's grub load is feeding the problem, we will say so at the survey and factor the advice in, rather than trap quietly and let the food restock the tunnels.

faqs.q: Our Duncan lawn was fine last year and is full of tunnels now. Did the moles move in from next door?
faqs.a: Effectively, yes. Moles disperse — especially young animals in the warm season — and a connected run of subdivision lawns is one hunting ground to them. A yard becomes the territory when its soil is loose, its topsoil stays moist, and its grub and worm population is rich, which describes a well-kept Duncan lawn laid over old pasture almost exactly. The campaign traps out the active system; keeping the address from being re-let is the food-and-moisture half of the plan, which is why we assess the lawn, not just the tunnels, on the first visit.

snake-removal.intro: Lyman is a Spartanburg County mill town on the Middle Tyger River — a compact community of mill-era homes in the river valley, with the wooded slopes of the Tyger's banks rising around it and mill ponds and creeks threaded through. Its snake work is valley work: watersnakes and racers along the river and the ponds, rat snakes in the mill cottages' crawlspaces and the older homes, and copperheads on the wooded slopes and in the stone and leaf litter where the town meets the hills. The river sets the baseline population; the housing stock — low rooflines, pier foundations, a century of additions — gives it access. Most Lyman calls are identification; the removals are the house snakes and the copperhead that has settled at a door.
snake-removal.extendedBody:
Tyger River valley, mill-town housing

Lyman's copperheads hold the slopes — the wooded banks above the river where stone, litter, and sun meet — and they come to houses at the slope's foot: the woodpile against the foundation, the brush at the fence line, the porch void. A copperhead established at the house ground is a removal, and the yard walk that follows it — piles moved, brush cut back, the seam between lawn and slope pushed uphill — is the prevention. The cottages' rat snakes are the valley's other constant: climbers in the crawlspaces and occasionally the attics, resident because rodents are, and removed with the rodent truth attached — seal the food in, and the next snake has no reason to apply. Watersnakes at the ponds and along the Tyger are identified and left, with the explanation given on the spot: they are the river's, they are harmless, and they are most of what the town calls about in the spring.

faqs.q: How much does snake removal cost in Lyman?
faqs.a: It depends on the species and the search — a rat snake found in a crawlspace is compact; a copperhead in a slope garden takes finding. Photograph first, from a safe distance: identification is free, and along the Tyger a large share of calls resolve as watersnakes left in peace. Removals are quoted before we come and include the habitat read — the woodpile, the brush line, the rodent sign in the crawlspace — because in a river valley the snake is the second half of every story.

faqs.q: Snakes keep appearing in our Lyman crawlspace. Why ours?
faqs.a: Because something under your house is feeding them — a crawlspace with a resident snake population has a resident rodent population first. Rat snakes and racers enter through the same unscreened vents and foundation gaps the mice use, and they stay for the hunting. The permanent fix is sequenced: the rodents addressed, the snakes removed, and the foundation sealed in the same programme — screened vents, gaps closed — so the crawlspace stops being a restaurant with rooms above it. Evicting snakes alone, into a stocked crawlspace, is a subscription; we will show you the sign and quote the whole sequence plainly.

mole-removal.intro: Wellford's moles work the same ground as Duncan's, one town east — Spartanburg County's I-85 corridor country of growth subdivisions laid over old pasture and field, where the graded topsoil and irrigated sod sit over soil that was feeding moles long before it was feeding lawns. Eastern moles surface their systems across Wellford's yards as ridged runs and rooted beds, following the worm-rich lines along the foundations, the drainage swales between the phases, and the old field edges the builders never erased. The calls are steady, seasonal, and honest work: a mole problem here is a food-and-soil fact expressed as tunnels, and it is managed as a campaign, not cured in a visit.
mole-removal.extendedBody:
Old pasture under new sod

The Wellford pattern starts with the ground's memory. Pasture soil carries deep worm populations and the loose structure moles prefer, and subdivision topsoil preserves both under a lawn that gets watered and fed — a combination that amounts to a maintained mole habitat with a house on it. Our work begins with the survey: active feeding runs distinguished from the deep highway tunnels along the foundations and swales, sets placed on the working system, and a checking cycle that moves the line as the sign moves. The programme is priced whole, in advance, because the honest unit of mole work is the campaign. And the lawn conversation is part of the fee: irrigation that keeps the topsoil wet all week and a heavy grub load are the two levers a homeowner controls, and on Wellford's connected lawns they decide whether a trapped-out system stays empty or is re-let by the next dispersing juvenile from two streets over. We will tell you plainly which lever your yard is suffering from — and which one is the neighbourhood's, beyond anyone's fence to fix.

faqs.q: How much does mole removal cost in Wellford?
faqs.a: It depends on the lot size and how much of the system is active — a single-yard programme is the standard unit; large corner lots with swale and foundation runs are longer campaigns. We survey and mark the active tunneling first, then quote the complete programme — sets, scheduled checks, and resets — as one firm price before any trap is placed. If the grub load is heavy, that finding is in the survey report, because trapping into a stocked pantry is how mole programmes get longer than they need to be.

faqs.q: Will the moles just come back after removal in Wellford?
faqs.a: They will try — the corridor's ground produces dispersing young moles every warm season, and a vacant, food-rich system is exactly what they are looking for. What the campaign buys is a yard that is no longer occupied and no longer expanding, and what keeps it that way is the food-and-moisture management we set out with the survey. There is an honest limit we will state: on connected subdivision lawns, no one can warrant the whole street. What we can warrant is the work — the active system trapped out, the progress shown at every check, and the advice that makes your yard the least attractive vacancy on the street.
